pieces.text: Colonial leaders formed the First Continental Congress in 1774 as a committee to respond to British taxes and to coordinate colonial resistance. In 1777, the Second Continental Congress drafted the

to provide a central government to manage the ongoing war. was a set of rules that organized a large area of land west of the Appalachian Mountains into a single territory. broke out in Massachusetts. Read about Shays's Rebellion. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In the 1780s, Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays returned home to his farm in western Massachusetts. He was shocked to discover that he was being called to court for not paying off his debts. Shays did not have the money to pay his debt because he had not yet been paid for serving as a soldier in the war. Shays was furious at being punished for not paying his debts, when the central government hadn't even paid what they owed him.

pieces.text: Many farmers in western Massachusetts were in the same situation as Shays. When the farmers could not pay their debts, the Massachusetts state courts began seizing the farmers' land and property. Shays and other farmers felt they had no choice but to use force. They marched to the courthouses with pitchforks, clubs, and muskets and refused to let the courts meet. Fearing the mobs, the Massachusetts governor assembled a
, or a group of volunteers who fight in emergencies, to fight the farmers. The battles between the state militia and the farmers ended with 4 dead and 20 wounded.

pieces.text: But before the states could meet,
broke out in Massachusetts. Read about Shays's Rebellion. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In the 1780s, Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays returned home to his farm in western Massachusetts. He was shocked to discover that he was being called to court for not paying off his debts. Shays did not have the money to pay his debt because he had not yet been paid for serving as a soldier in the war. Shays was furious at being punished for not paying his debts, when the central government hadn't even paid what they owed him.

pieces.text: Many farmers in western Massachusetts were in the same situation as Shays. When the farmers could not pay their debts, the Massachusetts state courts began seizing the farmers' land and property. Shays and other farmers felt they had no choice but to use force. They marched to the courthouses with pitchforks, clubs, and muskets and refused to let the courts meet. Fearing the mobs, the Massachusetts governor assembled a
, or a group of volunteers who fight in emergencies, to fight the farmers. The battles between the state militia and the farmers ended with 4 dead and 20 wounded.

pieces.text: During the Revolutionary War, the United States formed a national government under the Articles of Confederation. A

is a union of independent states with a common goal. The Articles of Confederation unified the states enough to win the war and achieve independence. But after the war, when the common goal became governing the new nation, the Articles of Confederation did not give enough power to the national government.

contents.text: The Articles of Confederation led to several problems for the new nation. Match each problem to the feature of the Articles of Confederation that caused it.

columnHeaders.text: Feature of the Articles of Confederation

draggableItems.text: States competed with each other for foreign trade advantages.
States could choose to ignore national laws.
The national government had no way to collect the money it needed to pay war debts.
Money from one state might not be accepted in another state.

staticItems.text: The Congress of the Confederation could pass laws, but didn't have the power to enforce them.
Only the states had the power to create taxes.
Each state could make its own trade agreements with other countries.
States could print their own paper money.

contents.text: Experiences from early in someone's life can shape his or her actions later in life. So, historians often consider a person's background when studying historical figures. Read about Washington's life and career before he became president. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: George Washington is born on a small plantation in a rural area of the Virginia Colony.

Washington's father dies, leaving a small farm and ten enslaved people to George Washington, and the Mount Vernon plantation to George's half-brother, Lawrence. Washington's formal education ends after his father's death.
Washington works as a land surveyor, earning a large income that allows him to purchase 1,500 acres of land, which becomes the basis for his wealth.
Washington joins the Virginia militia after Lawrence Washington's death. He also leases Mount Vernon from Lawrence's widow, Anne.
Lieutenant Colonel Washington leads an ambush of French forces in Pennsylvania, which helps spark the French and Indian War. The attack is widely reported in the colonies and in Europe.

Washington marries Martha Dandridge Custis, a widow who inherited a large plantation from her deceased husband. Combined with his existing land, this makes Washington one of the wealthiest men in Virginia.
Washington inherits Mount Vernon after Anne Washington dies. He eventually doubles both its size and its enslaved population.

subpoints.text: George Washington's family wealth depended on slavery, especially after his marriage to Martha Dandridge Custis. Washington voiced no concerns about the institution of slavery for much of his life. However, in his final decades, he began to oppose slavery for both financial and moral reasons. Though Washington privately opposed slavery, he publicly preferred a plan to gradually free enslaved people. After his death, Washington's will freed some of the enslaved people at Mount Vernon, but not those who legally belonged to the Custis family.

pieces.text: After the Revolutionary War, George Washington was celebrated across the new nation for his military leadership. He also earned praise after the war for demonstrating
, which are characteristics that help people navigate their disagreements, increase people's trust in government, or encourage people to place the good of the community over their own interests.

contents.text: Read the following passage about Washington's actions after the war. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: At the end of the war, George Washington disbanded the Continental Army and voluntarily stepped down from his position as commander in chief. Unlike other military leaders who used their wartime success to gain political power, Washington retired from politics and returned to his home in Mount Vernon. Leaders in the U.S. and overseas praised Washington's willingness to give up power. Some compared his retirement to that of the ancient Roman military and political leader Cincinnatus, who voluntarily surrendered absolute political power and retired to his farm.

After the war, Washington became the first president of the Society of the Cincinnati, a group of Revolutionary War veterans dedicated to upholding the ideals of the American Revolution. The society focused on protecting the political rights gained from the revolution, preserving the union of the states, and helping struggling veterans and their families.

contents.text: George Washington's retirement from public life after the Revolutionary War did not last long. In 1787, Washington joined delegates from 12 states at the Constitutional Convention, a meeting in Philadelphia to revise or replace the weak national government created by the Articles of Confederation. The delegates unanimously elected Washington as the president of the Constitutional Convention. Though others participated more in the convention's debates, Washington's opinion on the proposed Constitution carried great weight in the young nation.
Washington wrote a public letter stating his opinion of the Constitution. Read an excerpt of his letter. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: It is obviously impracticable in the federal government of these states, to secure all rights of independent
to each [state], and yet provide for the interest and safety of all.…

textContent.text: In all our deliberations on [the Constitution] we kept steadily in our view…the [strengthening] of our union, in which is involved our prosperity, [happiness], safety, perhaps our national existence.…and thus the Constitution, which we now present, is the result of a spirit of [friendship], and of that mutual deference and [compromise] which [our unique] political situation rendered [necessary].

That it will meet the full and entire [approval] of every state is not perhaps to be expected; but each [state] will doubtless consider that, had her interest alone been consulted, the consequences might have been particularly disagreeable or [harmful] to others.…

contents.text: Read the following passage about Washington's actions after the war. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: At the end of the war, George Washington disbanded the Continental Army and voluntarily stepped down from his position as commander in chief. Unlike other military leaders who used their wartime success to gain political power, Washington retired from politics and returned to his home in Mount Vernon. Leaders in the U.S. and overseas praised Washington's willingness to give up power. Some compared his retirement to that of the ancient Roman military and political leader Cincinnatus, who voluntarily surrendered absolute political power and retired to his farm.

After the war, Washington became the first president of the Society of the Cincinnati, a group of Revolutionary War veterans dedicated to upholding the ideals of the American Revolution. The society focused on protecting the political rights gained from the revolution, preserving the union of the states, and helping struggling veterans and their families.

contents.text: George Washington's retirement from public life after the Revolutionary War did not last long. In 1787, Washington joined delegates from 12 states at the Constitutional Convention, a meeting in Philadelphia to revise or replace the weak national government created by the Articles of Confederation. The delegates unanimously elected Washington as the president of the Constitutional Convention. Though others participated more in the convention's debates, Washington's opinion on the proposed Constitution carried great weight in the young nation.
Washington wrote a public letter stating his opinion of the Constitution. Match each excerpt of his letter with its meaning.

draggableItems.text: Though some states may disagree with parts of the Constitution, it will balance the interests of all the states.
It's not possible for each state to be fully independent while still having a federal government that is strong enough to protect its citizens.
At the Constitutional Convention, we focused on improving national unity, hoping to enhance our national wealth and security.
We are presenting a Constitution that is the product of many agreements among various state delegates.

staticItems.text: It is obviously impracticable in the federal government of these states, to secure all rights of independent [political authority] to each [state], and yet provide for the interest and safety of all.…

In all our deliberations on [the Constitution] we kept steadily in our view…the [strengthening] of our union, in which is involved our prosperity, [happiness], safety, perhaps our national existence.…
…and thus the Constitution, which we now present, is the result of a spirit of [friendship], and of that mutual deference and [compromise] which [our unique] political situation rendered [necessary].

That it will meet the full and entire [approval] of every state is not perhaps to be expected; but each [state] will doubtless consider that, had her interest alone been consulted, the consequences might have been particularly disagreeable or [harmful] to others.…

contents.text: Read the following passage about Washington's actions after the war. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: At the end of the war, George Washington disbanded the Continental Army and voluntarily stepped down from his position as commander in chief. Unlike other military leaders who used their wartime success to gain political power, Washington retired from politics and returned to his home in Mount Vernon. Leaders in the U.S. and overseas praised Washington's willingness to give up power. Some compared his retirement to that of the ancient Roman military and political leader Cincinnatus, who voluntarily surrendered absolute political power and retired to his farm.

After the war, Washington became the first president of the Society of the Cincinnati, a group of Revolutionary War veterans dedicated to upholding the ideals of the American Revolution. The society focused on protecting the political rights gained from the revolution, preserving the union of the states, and helping struggling veterans and their families.

contents.text: George Washington's retirement from public life after the Revolutionary War did not last long. In 1787, Washington joined delegates from 12 states at the Constitutional Convention, a meeting in Philadelphia to revise or replace the weak national government created by the Articles of Confederation. The delegates unanimously elected Washington as the president of the Constitutional Convention. Though others participated more in the convention's debates, Washington's opinion on the proposed Constitution carried great weight in the young nation.
Washington wrote a public letter stating his opinion of the Constitution. Read an excerpt of his letter. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: It is obviously impracticable in the federal government of these states, to secure all rights of independent
to each [state], and yet provide for the interest and safety of all.…

textContent.text: In all our deliberations on [the Constitution] we kept steadily in our view…the [strengthening] of our union, in which is involved our prosperity, [happiness], safety, perhaps our national existence.…and thus the Constitution, which we now present, is the result of a spirit of [friendship], and of that mutual deference and [compromise] which [our unique] political situation rendered [necessary].

That it will meet the full and entire [approval] of every state is not perhaps to be expected; but each [state] will doubtless consider that, had her interest alone been consulted, the consequences might have been particularly disagreeable or [harmful] to others.…

subpoints.text: George Washington's family wealth depended on slavery, especially after his marriage to Martha Dandridge Custis. Washington voiced no concerns about the institution of slavery for much of his life. However, in his final decades, he began to oppose slavery for both financial and moral reasons. Though Washington privately opposed slavery, he publicly preferred a plan to gradually free enslaved people. After his death, Washington's will freed some of the enslaved people at Mount Vernon, but not those who legally belonged to the Custis family.

pieces.text: George Washington is born on a small plantation in a rural area of the Virginia Colony.

Washington's father dies, leaving a small farm and ten enslaved people to George Washington, and the Mount Vernon plantation to George's half-brother, Lawrence. Washington's formal education ends after his father's death.
Washington works as a land surveyor, earning a large income that allows him to purchase 1,500 acres of land, which becomes the basis for his wealth.
Washington joins the Virginia militia after Lawrence Washington's death. He also leases Mount Vernon from Lawrence's widow, Anne.
Lieutenant Colonel Washington leads an ambush of French forces in Pennsylvania, which helps spark the French and Indian War. The attack is widely reported in the colonies and in Europe.

Washington marries Martha Dandridge Custis, a widow who inherited a large plantation from her deceased husband. Combined with his existing land, this makes Washington one of the wealthiest men in Virginia.
Washington inherits Mount Vernon after Anne Washington dies. He eventually doubles both its size and its enslaved population.

subpoints.text: George Washington's family wealth depended on slavery, especially after his marriage to Martha Dandridge Custis. Washington voiced no concerns about the institution of slavery for much of his life. However, in his final decades, he began to oppose slavery for both financial and moral reasons. Though Washington privately opposed slavery, he publicly preferred a plan to gradually free enslaved people. After his death, Washington's will freed some of the enslaved people at Mount Vernon, but not those who legally belonged to the Custis family.

contents.text: Read the following passage about Washington's actions after the war. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: At the end of the war, George Washington disbanded the Continental Army and voluntarily stepped down from his position as commander in chief. Unlike other military leaders who used their wartime success to gain political power, Washington retired from politics and returned to his home in Mount Vernon. Leaders in the U.S. and overseas praised Washington's willingness to give up power. Some compared his retirement to that of the ancient Roman military and political leader Cincinnatus, who voluntarily surrendered absolute political power and retired to his farm.

After the war, Washington became the first president of the Society of the Cincinnati, a group of Revolutionary War veterans dedicated to upholding the ideals of the American Revolution. The society focused on protecting the political rights gained from the revolution, preserving the union of the states, and helping struggling veterans and their families.

Scotland is part of Great Britain. So, even though M'Lean had documentation showing he was an American citizen, the commander claimed that M'Lean was actually British.
